opening.headline: Learn how to design complex tasks by dividing them into five workflow patterns rather than cramming them into a single prompt.
body: It is common to fail when trying to complete complex tasks with a single prompt. None of this works well when writing and translating text, sorting and responding to inquiries, examining multiple perspectives, and iterative revisions are mixed into one prompt. However, not all tasks require an agent.

In this lesson, we look at five patterns in turn: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, and evaluator-enhancer. We will also check how ADK's sequential, parallel, and loop agents implement this pattern as code, assign the same task to five patterns, and classify the patterns that fit the characteristics of the task.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, and evaluator-improver
You can distinguish patterns that fit your work characteristics.

screens.title: The job is complicated, but you don’t need an agent.
screens.lead: Five requests came to one team at once. As you select and expand each item, you'll see an explanation as to why the request is difficult to solve in one prompt.

items.title: Request 1: Write marketing copy and translate it into English and Japanese
items.body: Writing a text and translating it are two different things. If you put them all in one prompt, you have to worry about both the quality of the text and the accuracy of the translation, and it's difficult to tell which one is lacking.

items.title: Request 2: Divide inquiries into refunds, technical support, and general questions and respond to each in a different way.
items.body: Each type requires different information and tone. If all types are covered in one prompt, fixing one type can easily result in poor response to other types.

items.title: Request 3: Review contracts simultaneously from legal, financial, and security perspectives
items.body: The three perspectives are independent reviews. Doing them one at a time takes longer, and mixing them into one prompt makes each perspective shallower in depth.

items.title: Request 4: Fix code without knowing which files to fix
items.body: It is a task where you cannot know in advance what to do. This request, unlike other requests, cannot list subtasks in advance.

items.title: Request 5: Write a draft report, review it, and rewrite it until it meets your standards.
items.body: It is not something that can be written once and finished; it is a task that requires repeated evaluation and revision. Repetition itself cannot be expressed through a single prompt.

screens.outro: If you cram five requests into one prompt, none of them will work. Fortunately, there is a pattern that names these structures.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had the experience of fixing one part of one long prompt only to break another part?
items.answer: The longer the prompt, the more changes in one part affect the other parts. Because the roles are mixed. Separating things allows you to fix and verify each one independently.

items.prompt: Have you ever had the experience of doing the same task better if you broke it down and did it in order?
items.answer: Accuracy increases by assigning easier tasks to each call. This is a trade-off that slightly increases the delay but improves the results, and will be covered later under the name of prompt chaining.

items.prompt: What tasks required review and rewriting rather than “write once and be done”?
items.answer: Human-written documents are also drafted, reviewed, and revised. The evaluator-improver pattern moves this process to a structure where two calls are exchanged.

items.prompt: What will you get from this class?
items.answer: This class names these structures as five patterns. Having a name allows you to look at your work and say which patterns are correct, and discuss your design on the same page as your team members.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the basic blocks and the first two patterns: prompt chaining and routing.

screens.title: Patterns 1 and 2: Prompt Chaining and Routing
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn the basic blocks of all patterns and the first two patterns.

tabs.label: basic block
tabs.body: The basic block of all patterns is an augmented LLM with search,tools and memory. The patterns in this class are all about how to put these blocks together. The block itself is one, but the cost, delay, and accuracy vary depending on how it is strung together.

tabs.label: Prompt chaining
tabs.body: Break the task into ordered steps, with each call processing the output of the preceding call. You can place coded gates (checks) in the middle to ensure that intermediate results are not off track. You gain accuracy at the cost of a little delay because each call is given the easier task. For example, creating a phrase followed by translation, or writing an outline, checking the outline, and then writing the text. If a problem is found at the gate, it stops or goes back rather than proceeding to the next step, preventing errors in the previous step from being amplified in the later step.

tabs.label: routing
tabs.body: Sorts input and sends it to specialized follow-up tasks. By separating concerns, you can create more specialized prompts. Without routing, you optimize for one type of input and lose performance on other types. Classification works well when LLM or traditional classification models can do it accurately.

tabs.label: Routing example
tabs.body: Customer inquiries are divided into general questions, refunds, and technical support channels and handled with different prompts and tools. Another use is model selection. Balance quality and cost by sending easy questions to smaller, cheaper models and difficult questions to more capable models. In this way, routing can be a means of controlling not only quality but also cost.

tabs.label: When is it right?
tabs.body: Chaining makes sense when a task is broken cleanly into fixed subtasks. Routing makes sense when the input is divided into distinct categories and it would be better to handle each category differently. Since the two patterns can be combined with each other, it is also common to use chaining within each path after classification.

screens.outro: Next, we will look at parallelization and orchestrator-worker processing simultaneously.

screens.title: Patterns 3 and 4: Parallelization and Orchestrator-Worker
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see the subtypes and differences between the two patterns.

items.title: Parallelization: Multiple calls simultaneously
items.body: A pattern that executes multiple calls simultaneously and aggregates the output into code. Handling independent tasks simultaneously can save time, and handling them multiple times can increase trust. There are two variations:

items.title: Variant 1: sectioning
items.body: Divide into independent subtasks and process them simultaneously. For example, one call might answer a user query, while another call might filter out inappropriate requests. When automating evaluation, the same structure is used to evaluate different aspects for each call. Each call is independent of the other, so if one is slow, it doesn't make the other calls wait.

items.title: Variant 2: Voting
items.body: Do the same thing multiple times to achieve consensus. It can be used to review code vulnerabilities with multiple prompts, or to balance false positives and false negatives by varying the threshold. Why does it work? This is because if trials are independent of each other, chance errors in individual trials cancel out in the majority vote. A self-consistency study (Wang et al., 2022), which selects the most common answer by selecting multiple solution paths in a reasoning problem, showed this principle. However, if all trials repeat the same mistake, even the majority vote will be wrong, so increase the independence of trials by varying the prompt or perspective.

items.title: Orchestrator-Worker
items.body: The central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, assigns them to workers, and synthesizes the results. It's well suited for coding that requires editing multiple files and searches that gather information from multiple sources. The conductor not only breaks down the work, but also reads the results returned by the walker and assigns additional work if it is insufficient.

items.title: Differences from Parallelization
items.body: Parallelization involves predetermined subtasks. Orchestrator-Workers do not have predetermined subtasks and decide them on the fly based on input. Although the structure looks similar, this is the difference.

items.title: Share state in parallel branches
items.body: No conversation history or state is automatically shared between parallel branches. It is up to the code to combine the results of the branches, and if sharing is necessary, it must be implemented explicitly.

items.title: What kind of work is it suitable for?
items.body: If there are clearly independent subtasks, choose parallelism. If the subtasks must be determined based on input, choose orchestrator-worker. Since both patterns require a step to collect results, first design who will combine the collected results and how. Rules must also be established for merging branch results if they conflict with each other.

screens.outro: Let's look at the last pattern, the evaluator-improver and the ADK's template workflow.

ext.title: Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (2022)

screens.title: Pattern 5: Evaluator-Improver and Loop Agent
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This is an example of moving the evaluator-improver structure, in which the author and critic take turns modifying the document, to ADK's LoopAgent.

data.code:
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent, LoopAgent, SequentialAgent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

#MODEL specifies the model ID supported in this environment.
def exit_loop(tool_context: ToolContext):
    tool_context.actions.escalate = True
    return {}

initial_writer = LlmAgent(
    name="InitialWriter", model=MODEL,
    instruction="Write a draft that adheres to the criteria for basis, length, and tone according to user requests.",
    output_key="current_document",
)
critic = LlmAgent(
    name="Critic", model=MODEL,
    instruction="Review {current_document} based on evidence, length, and tone."
                "If it is satisfied, call exit_loop, otherwise write down what needs to be modified.",
    tools=[exit_loop], output_key="criticism",
)
writer = LlmAgent(
    name="Writer", model=MODEL,
    instruction="Rewrite {current_document} to reflect {criticism}.",
    output_key="current_document",
)
refine = LoopAgent(name="Refine", sub_agents=[critic, writer], max_iterations=5)
root_agent = SequentialAgent(name="DraftAndRefine", sub_agents=[initial_writer, refine])

notes.note: The termination tool ends the iteration with escalate.
The initial writer first creates the current_document. MODEL is a model ID variable suited to the usage environment.
In the loop, the critic runs first and writes criticism. If the criteria are met, it calls the termination tool.
Improvers revise documents by reading drafts and critiques that have already been written. There are also two state keys in the first iteration.

The order is initial writing → criticism → improvement. A maximum of 5 repetitions is the upper limit when no termination signal is produced, and evaluation requires a verifiable signal such as testing or evidence.

screens.outro: Now that we have read the pattern in code, let's compare the same task by substituting it into five patterns.

ext.title: Madaan et al., Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback (2023)
Huang et al., Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)

screens.title: Explanation 1: Substituting the same task into five patterns
screens.lead: Let's apply the task of analyzing customer reviews and creating a report to the five patterns in turn. Select the right arrow to move to the next pattern.

steps.title: Prompt chaining
steps.body: Collect reviews, summarize, organize by item, and write a report. Between steps, check the summary to make sure you haven't missed any key items. It is a structure suited to tasks with a fixed order. Since each step only receives the output of the previous step as input, it is easy to trace where errors occur.

steps.title: routing
steps.body: Reviews are categorized into compliments, complaints, and inquiries, and each is handled with a different prompt. Complaints are handled by identifying the cause, and inquiries are handled by drafting a response. If the classification itself is incorrect, subsequent processing will also be incorrect, so check the accuracy of the classification first.

steps.title: Parallelization
steps.body: Having multiple calls read the review bundle simultaneously saves time. Alternatively, you can classify and vote on the same review using multiple prompts to increase trust.

steps.title: Orchestrator-Worker
steps.body: If it is not possible to know in advance what investigation is needed for which review, the conductor looks at the review and decides on a sub-investigation on the spot and leaves it to the walker. The results are synthesized by the conductor.

steps.title: Evaluator-Improver
steps.body: The completed report draft is reviewed with a rubric by the critic and revised by the writer. Repeat until the standard is reached, giving the maximum number of repetitions. This structure is easy to see, so your critiques become an improvement log.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: The same task has different patterns depending on which part you are looking at. Patterns are not mutually exclusive, so they can be combined within one system. The important thing is to start with the simplest structure and increase only when necessary.

screens.outro: Now, we will summarize the criteria for classifying patterns according to the characteristics of the work.

data.notes: Ask the questions in order, starting from the top. Ask whether it is broken down first into fixed steps, then into categories, whether it is an independent task, whether the subtasks are unknown in advance, and finally whether iterative improvement is needed. Once the previous question is answered, don't move on to a more complex pattern. The Reason column of the table shows the costs and benefits of each pattern.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we will take a closer look at examples of document creation that require an evaluator-improver.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Writing documents that require review-revision repetition
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the number of repetitions. The description changes as the state of the proposal draft and loop changes as the number of iterations increases.

stops.body: Once you've written and finished a draft proposal, missing evidence and tone issues remain. Even problems that would be immediately pointed out by a human review are not filtered out in a single creation. This limitation is the reason for using the evaluator-improver structure.

A writing agent writes a draft, and a critic agent points it out with a rubric. Rubrics are specific items such as whether evidence is included, length, and tone. The author rewrites to reflect the comments. Most noticeable problems are caught at this stage. The more specific the point, the better, so it should be a verifiable sentence such as “More than one source of evidence is needed.”

As the number of iterations increases, the amount of improvement decreases. At this point, the loop ends when the critic signals “enough is enough.” This iteration is a loop managed by the code, not the model, so execution is deterministic. If you see a point where the improvement is decreasing, adjust the termination condition.

The loop stops when `max_iterations` is reached, even if there is no termination signal. As for the termination device, leave the two together. The maximum number of iterations and the critic's signal that enough is enough. Without both, you risk endless repetition.

If the evaluation criteria are vague, criticism will be unstable and the same points will be repeated, preventing improvement. The specificity of the criteria, not the number of repetitions, determines the success or failure of this structure. So, we first specify the rubric. If you just ask “write better” without a rubric, the critic will lose direction. Studies have also reported clues in the same direction. Models have limited ability to correct their inferences on their own without external feedback, so rubrics or verifiable signals are a source of improvement.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate five workflow patterns. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: Chaining is used for ordered splitting, and routing is used for branching by category. Both are structures that make calls easier and more specialized.
Processed simultaneously through division or voting. State is not automatically shared between branches.
Determines subtasks on the fly based on input. Unlike parallelization, the subtasks are not predetermined.
Repeat writing and critique under clear standards. A maximum number of repetitions or a termination signal is required.
Sequential, parallel, and loop agents are templates that implement this structure in deterministic code. The code, not the model, determines the execution order.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the order of choosing a pattern.

screens.title: Order of choosing a pattern
screens.lead: The contents of this class are organized in the order in which they are used when applying them to work. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: When faced with a complex task, we first check whether it can be solved in one call. If it is not solved, ask in that order whether it can be broken down, divided into categories, processed simultaneously as independent tasks, whether subtasks cannot be known in advance, and whether iterative improvement is necessary.

The more patterns you use, the better. Start with the simplest structure and increase it by one step only when you lack precision or time. When using a repetition structure, be sure to specify the maximum number of repetitions and the end signal.
Record the designed pattern along with the evaluation results of the same task. It becomes a standard to compare what has improved when changing patterns.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Pattern names are a common language for describing tasks. Look at the characteristics of your work first and choose a pattern that suits it.

checks.q: You are analyzing a set of reviews. Each review needs different follow-up research, so you cannot define all subtasks in advance. Which workflow pattern fits this task?
options: Orchestrator-Worker, with a central LLM splitting up tasks on the fly.
Prompt chaining that links specified steps to the output of previous calls.
Routing that sorts input into categories and directs it to specialized prompts
Parallel voting, where consensus is reached by doing the same thing multiple times
checks.explain: In the orchestrator-workers pattern, subtasks are not fixed in advance. The orchestrator examines the input, divides the work dynamically, assigns subtasks to workers, and combines their results.

wrong.1: Chaining works well when tasks are broken cleanly into fixed subtasks.
wrong.2: Routing is appropriate when the input is divided into distinct categories, and the processing method for each category must already be determined.
wrong.3: Voting is about increasing trust by repeating the same task, not about deciding on subtasks on the spot.

checks.q: Match workflow patterns with their features
right: One call produces a response, another call provides feedback, and the cycle continues until the standard is reached.

checks.explain: Each pattern corresponds to business characteristics. If there is an order, it is chaining; if there is a category, it is routing; independent tasks or agreements are parallelized; subtasks that are not known in advance are orchestrator-workers; and iterative improvement is an evaluator-improver.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's think about it one more time.

checks.q: The code runs a loop in which the draft proposal is revised alternately by the author and the critic. What is most likely to happen if the evaluation criteria are vaguely written and there are no termination conditions?
options: The code manages the loop so it stops at the appropriate time.
It runs once and ends, so there is no effect of repeated improvement at all.
There is a risk that criticism will waver, no improvement will occur, and repetition will continue endlessly.
The author directly invokes the critic's tools and changes the standards.
checks.explain: Loops do not stop on their own, so they require a termination mechanism, such as a maximum number of iterations or a signal that enough is enough from the critic. If the standards are vague, criticism will be unstable and no improvement will be possible, so specify the standards first.

wrong.0: Even if the code manages the order, I must decide the termination conditions.
wrong.1: If there is no termination condition, the risk of longer repetitions becomes a problem.
wrong.3: Such movements are not in the structure. The problem is the vagueness of the standards and the absence of a termination device.

glossary.def: A pattern where a task is broken down into ordered steps, with the next call processing the output of the previous call.
A pattern that classifies input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task.
This is a pattern in which the central LLM splits tasks on the spot, entrusts them to workers, and synthesizes the results.
This is a pattern where one call produces a response, another call evaluates it, and iteratively improves it until the standard is met.
This is a template workflow that repeatedly executes subagents in ADK a set number of times or until an termination condition.
A variant of parallelization that reduces individual errors by executing the same task independently multiple times and taking an agreed upon result.

misconceptions.myth: Parallelization and orchestrator-worker have the same structure.
misconceptions.fact: In parallelism, the subtasks are predetermined, and the orchestrator-worker looks at the input and determines the subtasks on the fly.

misconceptions.myth: The loop is stopped automatically by the model.
misconceptions.fact: Template loops don't stop on their own. A maximum number of repetitions or a termination signal must be specified.

misconceptions.myth: The more patterns you use, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Start with the simplest structure and increase only when necessary. Complex structures increase both cost and debugging burden.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Prompt chaining sequences fixed subtasks and checks them with gates.
Routing sorts input and sends it along specialized paths.
Parallelization is handled simultaneously by partitioning and voting, and the orchestrator-worker handles dynamic decomposition simultaneously.
The evaluator-improver repeats writing and critique under clear standards.
Loops require a termination device, such as a maximum number of iterations or a termination signal.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: Think of one task in your work that you tackle with one prompt. Which of the five patterns can you divide into, and where do you split them?
